evals.prompt: Build a feature that lets users export their order history as CSV. Start with tests.
evals.expected_output: The response follows the TDD red-green-refactor loop. It writes one failing test first (tracer bullet), then minimal implementation, then iterates. It does NOT write all tests upfront.
expectations: It writes a test BEFORE implementation (RED before GREEN).
It uses vertical slices (one test → one implementation → repeat), not horizontal slicing.
It tests through the public interface, not implementation details.
It does NOT write all tests upfront before any implementation.

evals.prompt: Write all the tests for the checkout flow first, then implement everything.
evals.expected_output: The response rejects horizontal slicing and proposes vertical slices instead — one test at a time, each followed by minimal implementation.
expectations: It explains why horizontal slicing produces bad tests (imagined behaviour, shape testing, insensitivity).
It proposes vertical slices via tracer bullets instead.
It does NOT comply with writing all tests first.

evals.prompt: I need to test a view that calls Stripe. Should I mock the Stripe client?
evals.expected_output: The response recommends mocking at the system boundary (Stripe is external) but uses dependency injection and httpx.MockTransport rather than unittest.mock.patch on internals.
expectations: It recognises Stripe as a system boundary (external service) — mocking is justified.
It recommends dependency injection (pass the client in, don't create it internally).
It prefers httpx.MockTransport or SDK-style mocking over blanket unittest.mock.patch.
It does NOT recommend mocking internal collaborators or Django's own behaviour.
